title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 33
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Fixing the Image
passages.text:
A. The difficult part of photography was never the image. A darkened room with a small aperture projects an inverted picture of whatever is outside, and this was known and used for centuries by astronomers and painters. What nobody could do was make the picture stay. The problem was chemical, not optical, and the whole delay in the medium's arrival lies in that distinction.

B. Early successes were undermined by the same reaction that produced them. Substances that darken in light will keep darkening, so an image that appeared would continue developing until it was uniformly black, and the crucial invention was not the capture but the fixing — a treatment that removed the remaining sensitive material and left what had already formed. Photography begins with the ability to stop a process rather than to start one.

C. Two rival methods established the medium with opposite properties. One produced a single unrepeatable plate of extraordinary detail; the other produced a negative from which any number of prints could be made, at some cost in sharpness. The second won, and the reason was reproducibility rather than quality — a decision about what the medium was for that has shaped every later stage of it.

D. Exposure times determined subject matter far more than taste did. When a portrait required the subject to remain still for minutes, photography could record buildings, landscapes and rigid seated figures and nothing else; the solemnity of early portraits is a technical artefact read ever since as a period mood. As exposures shortened, movement, candour and eventually the unposed instant became available, and each was described at the time as a new artistic intention.

E. The claim to truthfulness was contested from the beginning, which the medium's later reputation obscures. Photographs were being staged, combined, retouched and captioned misleadingly within a few years of becoming practical, and the belief that a photograph could not lie was never held by the people making them. What made them persuasive was not accuracy but the appearance of having required no interpretation.

F. Digital capture changed the economics and left the ambiguity intact. The marginal cost of an exposure fell to nothing, so the number of images made rose beyond any possibility of being looked at, and the constraint moved from making pictures to finding them again. Manipulation became easier and also more detectable, and the question of whether an image records something has become a question about its provenance rather than about the image itself.

passages.title: The Skeleton Is Not Scaffolding
passages.text:
Bone is often imagined as an inert framework, like the timber inside a building, and almost nothing about how it behaves fits that picture. It is living tissue with its own blood supply, continuously dismantled and rebuilt by two opposing cell populations, and a skeleton replaces a substantial proportion of its material over a decade. What looks like a fixed structure is a slow equilibrium between removal and replacement.

That equilibrium responds to mechanical loading, which is the central fact with the widest consequences. Bone laid down where stress is high and removed where it is low means the skeleton adapts its shape and density to the forces it actually experiences, and the adaptation is specific to the site loaded rather than general. This is why the racket arm of a lifelong tennis player has measurably denser bone than the other, and why exercise that does not load a region does little for it.

The kind of loading matters more than the amount. Bone responds to strain that is unusual in magnitude or direction and rapidly stops responding to repetition of the familiar, so activity that is varied, brief and vigorous produces more adaptation than a much larger volume of steady comfortable movement. Jumping and changes of direction do more for bone than a long walk, and this has been demonstrated repeatedly in trials rather than merely inferred.

The clinical importance lies in what happens when loading is removed. Prolonged bed rest and time in weightlessness both produce rapid bone loss, in a pattern that mirrors the adaptation working in reverse, and the loss is fastest in exactly the sites that normally bear most weight. The skeleton is not conserving material against future need; it is disinvesting from a structure the body has been informed is unnecessary.

Age complicates the picture without changing the principle. The balance between removal and replacement shifts with age and with hormonal change, so the same loading produces less gain, but it continues to produce gain — the response is attenuated rather than absent. Trials in older adults find that appropriate loading slows loss and sometimes reverses part of it, and that the effect disappears when the loading stops, which is true of every adaptation of this kind.

The practical conclusion is less appealing than a pharmaceutical one and better supported than most of what is sold on the subject. Bone density is not principally a matter of calcium intake, which matters only when it is deficient, and supplementation in people already adequately supplied does not build bone. What builds bone is loading it, which is free, requires effort, and cannot be delegated to a product.

passages.title: Prices Without a Market
passages.text:
The market for art violates almost every condition that makes prices informative. Each object is unique, so there is no comparable item whose price could anchor a valuation; transactions are infrequent and often private; the same object may not trade again for decades; and a substantial part of what is being purchased is the expectation of what others will later think it is worth. Prices exist, and what they are prices of is a genuinely difficult question.

Authentication is the foundation and it is less secure than the sums involved suggest. Attribution rests on documented history of ownership, on physical analysis, and on expert judgement, and the three can conflict. Scientific tests can establish that materials are consistent with a period and cannot establish who applied them; a documented history can be fabricated; and expert opinion has been demonstrably wrong in both directions often enough that the market has largely stopped relying on it alone.

Scarcity in this market is unusual because it is absolute and retrospective. The supply of work by any dead artist is fixed, so demand can only express itself in price, and an artist's reputation can rise or fall long after the work is finished with no possibility of the supply responding. This makes the market a pure measure of shifting opinion, and explains why value can move enormously without anything about the object changing.

Intermediaries occupy a position that would be considered untenable in a regulated market. Dealers advise buyers, hold inventory of the artists they promote, and shape the reputations that determine the value of what they hold; auction houses advise sellers on estimates, guarantee minimum prices, and sometimes hold a financial interest in the outcome. None of this is concealed, and the conflicts are structural rather than the result of misconduct.

Art as an investment performs worse than its promoters claim and differently from how it is measured. Published indices are built from works that came to auction, which excludes those that failed to sell and those whose owners saw no point in offering them, and the resulting figures inherit a survivorship bias that is difficult to correct. Holding costs — insurance, storage, conservation — are substantial and rarely deducted, and the asset generates no income while held.

What the market does supply is worth stating without cynicism, because the criticisms above are frequently taken to condemn the whole activity. It moves objects to people who want them, funds living artists indirectly through the reputations it builds, and finances institutions that would otherwise not exist. Its prices are poor measures of aesthetic worth and were never intended to be, and the mistake is not the market's but the reading of its prices as a verdict.
